summary: In Greek mythology, Nicostratus was a son of Menelaus, king of Sparta. Sources disagree whether his mother was Helen or a slave woman. Hesiod and the epic poet Cinaethon knew him; Pausanias makes him and Megapenthes illegitimate sons who, according to the Rhodians, drove Helen from Sparta while Orestes still wandered.
etymology: Ancient Greek Νικόστρατος (Nikóstratos), "Victorious Army" — a name that suggests his birth after the Trojan War.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Although Homer's Odyssey names Hermione as the only child of Menelaus and Helen, other sources mention a son Nicostratus. Apollodorus reports that Menelaus had by Helen a daughter Hermione and, according to some, a son Nicostratus. A scholium on Sophocles' Electra quotes Hesiod: Helen bore Hermione to Menelaus, and last of all Nicostratus, scion of Ares.

According to Pausanias, Nicostratus and Megapenthes were sons of Menelaus by a slave; because they were illegitimate, Agamemnon's son Orestes succeeded Menelaus as king of Sparta. One account says the Lacedaemonians worshipped Nicostratus and Aithiolas, two sons of Helen.

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: According to the Rhodians, when Orestes was still wandering under the Erinyes after killing Clytemnestra, Nicostratus and Megapenthes drove Helen out; she found refuge on Rhodes with Polyxo.
Pausanias records that Nicostratus and Megapenthes were depicted riding a single horse on the sixth-century BC throne of Apollo at Amyclae, designed by Bathycles of Magnesia.
